content: Placenta cord banking involves the collection and storage of stem cells derived from the placenta, in addition to those obtained from umbilical cord blood, following the birth of a baby. Placental stem cells are exclusively found in the placenta and are collected after the umbilical cord blood has been drawn. These stem cells are non-embryonic, similar to those obtained from umbilical cord blood. Both the placenta and the umbilical cord are rich sources of stem cells. Collecting and preserving stem cells from the placenta, in addition to those from cord blood, significantly increases the total number of prenatal stem cells available for future use. The placenta is a particularly rich source of CD34+ stem cells. By banking both placental and cord blood stem cells, the total number of CD34+ stem cells collected is, on average, doubled. While umbilical cord blood is collected by healthcare providers at the hospital, the placenta must be sent to a laboratory for processing before the stem cells can be extracted. This makes the collection and processing of placental stem cells more labor-intensive compared to cord blood stem cell processing. Both placental and cord blood stem cell units undergo processing to remove red blood cells and are then cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen tanks at a temperature of -196 degrees Celsius. These stem cell units are stored in two separate cryopreservation bags, resulting in two distinct stem cell units. Cord blood stem cells have been used to treat over 80 diseases, including leukemia, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and sickle cell anemia. Placental stem cells can be used in combination with cord blood stem cells to enhance engraftment potential by increasing the total number of stem cells, including CD34+ stem cells.
